chunk_findings.detail: This test claims to prove that a worker frame with an unknown request id does not cause the original client call to be lost, but it never checks that the original call (`id=1`) is answered. It sends `x/bad` with id `1`, then only asserts that a later `ping` with id `2` gets a reply. If the shim drops the pending `id=1` request or leaves it unanswered, the test still passes because the ping reply satisfies it, giving false confidence against calls left unanswered.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_mcp_soft_shim.py:test_an_answer_for_an_unknown_request_id_is_dropped_and_the_call_is_not_lost

chunk_findings.detail: `reap` waits at most 5s and, on `subprocess.TimeoutExpired`, only calls `kill()` and returns. It never `wait()`s again, so `returncode` stays `None` and the child is left as a zombie. A worker that does not exit within 5s (blocked in uninterruptible I/O, or a full stdout pipe so it does not observe stdin close until `SIGKILL`) is the input: after `kill()` the shim still has an unreaped process. On a long-lived MCP session that restarts workers, those zombies accumulate, and any later exit path that treats `returncode is None` as "still running" can wait forever.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/mcpshim/child.py:reap

chunk_findings.detail: `run` treats every exception from `handle` as a logged no-op, so the client request is never answered. A snapshot `S.read` returns as fresh, client-matched, and in age, but with `protocols` missing or `[]`, makes `servable` raise `KeyError`/`IndexError` on `data["protocols"][0]` during `initialize`; the same swallow hits `tools/list` if `S.tools_list_result` raises. The JSON-RPC request stays outstanding for the life of the connection.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/mcpshim/shim.py:99

chunk_findings.detail: Hostile worker frames are applied with no shape or id check. `{"t":"note","msg":{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":<client id>,"result":{}}}` is written straight to the client, so an in-flight call is answered early and then answered again when the real `res` arrives. A `res` whose `msg` is not a dict (for example `[]`) hits `reply.get` and raises `AttributeError` on the reader callback; that frame’s client id is not replaced with `cid`, so a `msg.id` of another outstanding call attributes the result to the wrong request.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/mcpshim/shim.py:266

chunk_findings.detail: `notifications/cancelled` (and `notifications/initialized`) are dropped and never forwarded. After `tools/call` id 7 is in `pending`, a cancel for that id returns immediately; the worker still runs and `on_frame` writes a result for id 7, so the client is answered for a call it cancelled.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/mcpshim/shim.py:130

chunk_findings.detail: `find_repo` treats a non-absolute `git rev-parse --git-common-dir` result as relative to `where`, but Git prints that path relative to the process cwd (and does not get `--path-format=absolute`). With cwd `/tmp`, `DDFLOW_REPO=[REDACTED:path]`, and stdout `../home/proj/.git` (or `home/proj/.git`), the join is `(Path("[REDACTED:path]") / that).resolve().parent`, which is not `[REDACTED:path]`. The shim then reads or writes the snapshot under the wrong tree (or a path that does not exist) instead of the checkout the docstring claims to return. The same return also uses `.parent` of the common git dir, so a submodule or `--separate-git-dir` layout is wrong even when the path is absolute.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/mcpshim/wire.py:find_repo

chunk_findings.detail: The new stall timer can kill a worker after `send` has already succeeded, because `stall.cancel()` cannot stop a `Timer` callback that has already started. If a large frame makes `write`/`flush` take about `hello_timeout_s` (which is floored at 0.1 s), the timer may expire just as `flush()` returns. The `finally` block then calls `stall.cancel()`, but `self.kill` may already be running or about to run, so the worker is killed even though `send` returns `True`. The shim therefore treats the frame as accepted while the worker is being killed before processing it, leaving the corresponding client request unanswered or answered only after a later failure path.

chunk_findings.detail: The new assertion `assert wire.read_line(io.StringIO("x" * 20 + "\n"), 10) == ("", wire.OVERSIZE_PENDING)` is wrong for the current `wire.read_line`: the line is complete (`complete` is `True`), its encoded size is 21, so `size - complete > limit` is true and the function returns `("", wire.OVERSIZE_DONE)`, not `OVERSIZE_PENDING`. This makes the new test fail on an input that is already a complete oversize line.

chunk_findings.detail:
`test_read_line_reports_each_kind_of_oversize` asserts `wire.read_line(io.StringIO("x" * 20 + "
"), 10) == ("", wire.OVERSIZE_PENDING)`. That input is a finished line: `readline` returns `"x"*20+"
"`, `endswith("
")` is true, and `size - complete` is 20, which is over the limit, so `read_line` returns `("", OVERSIZE_DONE)`. The new test therefore fails on collect/run. Treating that frame as pending would also be the wrong contract: the newline was already consumed, so a caller that then `discard_line`s would drop the next message.

chunk_findings.detail: `Worker.send` performs an unbounded blocking `write`/`flush` while holding `self.wlock`. If a worker process is alive but stops reading stdin (wedged, busy loop, internal queue full, etc.), the OS pipe buffer fills after a modest amount of data (typically ~64 KiB on Linux). At that point `self.proc.stdin.write(...)` or `flush()` can block indefinitely, holding `self.wlock` forever. Any other thread that tries to send, and any shutdown path that expects to stop the worker, can hang; `reap`’s attempt to close stdin is not a reliable way to unblock a blocked `TextIOWrapper` write. There is no write timeout or non-blocking handling.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/mcpshim/child.py:62-69

chunk_findings.detail: `Worker.reap` closes `self.proc.stdin` without acquiring `self.wlock`. Concrete race: thread A is inside `Worker.send`, writing a large JSON-RPC frame to the worker; thread B calls `reap` because of client EOF, worker exit, or shim shutdown. Closing the stdin pipe while `send` is in progress can leave a partial JSON line already flushed to the worker and discard the rest, or raise after partial data has been written. `send` catches the exception and returns `False`, but the worker’s input stream is now desynchronized, so later frames may be misparsed or misattributed. `reap` must stop sends (e.g. hold `self.wlock`) before closing stdin.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/mcpshim/child.py:77-86

chunk_findings.detail: If `self.proc.wait(timeout=5)` times out, `reap` calls `self.kill()` and then returns without waiting for the killed process. The child may remain a zombie (or, if kill fails, still running) after `reap` returns, even though the shim may now believe the worker is fully stopped. Example: a worker ignores SIGTERM, `wait(5)` times out, `kill()` sends SIGKILL, but no final `wait()` reaps the process table entry.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/mcpshim/child.py:83-86

chunk_findings.detail: `clamp` accepts arbitrarily small positive values for `restart_window_s` because the only lower check for that key is “finite and not exactly zero.” A tampered snapshot can contain `{"limits": {"restart_window_s": 1e-9, "restart_max": 20}}`; `limits_for` will return `restart_window_s = 1e-9`. If the shim’s restart limiter uses that window to decide whether `restart_max` restarts have happened recently, worker spawn/initialize time is orders of magnitude larger than 1e-9 seconds, so earlier restart timestamps expire before the next spawn and the limiter never reaches `restart_max`. A smaller accepted value such as `5e-324` is even worse: `time.monotonic() + 5e-324` is indistinguishable from `time.monotonic()` at normal monotonic values, making the window effectively zero. This defeats the restart-window rate limit and can allow repeated worker spawns.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/mcpshim/limits.py:clamp

chunk_findings.detail: `read_line` can hang indefinitely on a malformed oversize client line. With `limit=1024`, if a client sends 2048 bytes of `x` with no newline and then keeps stdin open, the first `stream.readline(limit + 1)` returns a 1025-character string without a newline, so the code enters the drain loop at `wire.py:46` and blocks in `stream.readline(65536)` waiting for either a newline or EOF. Because the reader thread never returns to its loop, the shim cannot process shutdown or answer pending calls; the client can hold the connection open forever and wedge the shim.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/mcpshim/wire.py:45

chunk_findings.detail: `find_repo` runs `git` with the shim’s stdin inherited. `subprocess.run(..., capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=10)` does not set `stdin=subprocess.DEVNULL`, so the child can read the MCP client’s stdin pipe. If the environment/PATH supplied to the shim contains a `git` wrapper that reads stdin (for example a malicious or misconfigured wrapper behaving like `cat`), the wrapper consumes client JSON-RPC lines before the shim’s reader can see them; with the 10-second timeout, startup stalls and the consumed initialize/request bytes are lost.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/mcpshim/wire.py:27

chunk_findings.detail: `find_repo` can crash on a path whose bytes are not valid in the locale encoding. On POSIX, if `DDFLOW_REPO` (or the current directory passed as `start`) points to a directory name containing bytes invalid in the locale, `git` may echo that path in stdout/stderr. Because `subprocess.run(..., text=True)` decodes strictly, it can raise `UnicodeDecodeError`, which is a `ValueError` and is not caught by `except (OSError, subprocess.SubprocessError)`. The shim then dies instead of falling back to `where.resolve()`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/mcpshim/wire.py:29

chunk_findings.detail: The fixture docstring advertises a plain `badid` mode that answers with an unknown frame id, but the implementation gates it with `mode_for("badid", method)`, which requires the exact mode string `badid:<method>`. If a test sets `FAKE_MODE=badid` as documented and sends a request, `mode_for` returns false, `rid` remains `frame["id"]`, and the worker replies with the correct id; the unknown-frame-id path is never exercised.
chunk_findings.title: tests/fixtures/mcp_shim/fake_worker.py:66 (`serve`)

chunk_findings.detail: The assertion line beginning `assert any(t["name"] == "ddflow_brief" ...` is syntactically invalid as written: the `any(` call is never closed and the line contains no valid complete expression. This makes the test module fail to import/collect with a `SyntaxError`, so none of the security/robustness tests in this file can run.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_mcp_soft_shim.py:test_a_real_worker_serves_a_session_and_the_next_one_needs_none

chunk_findings.detail: This test claims to prove that a worker frame with an unknown request id does not cause the original client call to be lost, but it never checks that the original call (`id=1`) is answered. It sends `x/bad` with id `1`, then only asserts that a later `ping` with id `2` gets a reply. If the shim drops the pending `id=1` request or leaves it unanswered, the test still passes because the ping reply satisfies it, giving false confidence against calls left unanswered.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_mcp_soft_shim.py:test_an_answer_for_an_unknown_request_id_is_dropped_and_the_call_is_not_lost

chunk_findings.detail: `reap` waits at most 5s and, on `subprocess.TimeoutExpired`, only calls `kill()` and returns. It never `wait()`s again, so `returncode` stays `None` and the child is left as a zombie. A worker that does not exit within 5s (blocked in uninterruptible I/O, or a full stdout pipe so it does not observe stdin close until `SIGKILL`) is the input: after `kill()` the shim still has an unreaped process. On a long-lived MCP session that restarts workers, those zombies accumulate, and any later exit path that treats `returncode is None` as "still running" can wait forever.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/mcpshim/child.py:reap

chunk_findings.detail: `run` treats every exception from `handle` as a logged no-op, so the client request is never answered. A snapshot `S.read` returns as fresh, client-matched, and in age, but with `protocols` missing or `[]`, makes `servable` raise `KeyError`/`IndexError` on `data["protocols"][0]` during `initialize`; the same swallow hits `tools/list` if `S.tools_list_result` raises. The JSON-RPC request stays outstanding for the life of the connection.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/mcpshim/shim.py:99

chunk_findings.detail: Hostile worker frames are applied with no shape or id check. `{"t":"note","msg":{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":<client id>,"result":{}}}` is written straight to the client, so an in-flight call is answered early and then answered again when the real `res` arrives. A `res` whose `msg` is not a dict (for example `[]`) hits `reply.get` and raises `AttributeError` on the reader callback; that frame’s client id is not replaced with `cid`, so a `msg.id` of another outstanding call attributes the result to the wrong request.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/mcpshim/shim.py:266

chunk_findings.detail: `notifications/cancelled` (and `notifications/initialized`) are dropped and never forwarded. After `tools/call` id 7 is in `pending`, a cancel for that id returns immediately; the worker still runs and `on_frame` writes a result for id 7, so the client is answered for a call it cancelled.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/mcpshim/shim.py:130

chunk_findings.detail: `find_repo` treats a non-absolute `git rev-parse --git-common-dir` result as relative to `where`, but Git prints that path relative to the process cwd (and does not get `--path-format=absolute`). With cwd `/tmp`, `DDFLOW_REPO=[REDACTED:path]`, and stdout `../home/proj/.git` (or `home/proj/.git`), the join is `(Path("[REDACTED:path]") / that).resolve().parent`, which is not `[REDACTED:path]`. The shim then reads or writes the snapshot under the wrong tree (or a path that does not exist) instead of the checkout the docstring claims to return. The same return also uses `.parent` of the common git dir, so a submodule or `--separate-git-dir` layout is wrong even when the path is absolute.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/mcpshim/wire.py:find_repo

chunk_findings.detail: The new stall timer can kill a worker after `send` has already succeeded, because `stall.cancel()` cannot stop a `Timer` callback that has already started. If a large frame makes `write`/`flush` take about `hello_timeout_s` (which is floored at 0.1 s), the timer may expire just as `flush()` returns. The `finally` block then calls `stall.cancel()`, but `self.kill` may already be running or about to run, so the worker is killed even though `send` returns `True`. The shim therefore treats the frame as accepted while the worker is being killed before processing it, leaving the corresponding client request unanswered or answered only after a later failure path.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/mcpshim/child.py:send

chunk_findings.detail: The new note guard and answer-id rewrite still assume `frame["msg"]` exists and is a mapping. A worker frame `{"t":"note","msg":[]}` (or missing `msg`, or `"msg": null`) reaches `msg = frame["msg"]` and then `msg.get("method")`, raising `AttributeError`/`KeyError` before the intended “dropped note” log can run. Likewise, a worker frame `{"t":"res","id":<rid>,"msg":[]}` reaches `reply = {**frame["msg"], "id": cid}` and raises `TypeError` before the pending entry can be popped and answered. If the worker-reader callback is not guarded, this kills the reader; if it is guarded, the client request associated with `<rid>` is left unanswered. This is the non-mapping/shape-check part of previous finding #13 that the new probes do not cover.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/mcpshim/shim.py:on_frame

chunk_findings.detail:
Forcing UTF-8 with `errors="replace"` can turn a previously fatal decode into a silently wrong repository path. On POSIX, a repository directory name may contain bytes that are valid filesystem bytes but invalid UTF-8 (for example `DDFLOW_REPO=/tmp/proj-\xff`). `git rev-parse --git-common-dir` prints that path as raw bytes, but `subprocess.run(..., encoding="utf-8", errors="replace")` decodes it to `/tmp/proj-
/.git` (with U+FFFD). Since `returncode == 0` and stdout is non-empty, the function returns the resolved parent of that corrupted path instead of falling back to `where.resolve()`, so the shim then uses a nonexistent/wrong snapshot root. The robust fallback should be used when the decoded Git output cannot be mapped back to the actual filesystem path (for example by using binary output and `os.fsdecode`, or by verifying the resulting path exists).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/mcpshim/wire.py:find_repo

chunk_findings.detail: The oversize-line fix moved the blocking drain out of `read_line`, but the replacement `discard_line` is still an unbounded blocking loop. The new `read_line` contract says the rest of an oversize line is unread and `discard_line` skips it. If a client sends `limit + 1` bytes with no newline and then keeps the connection open (or keeps sending data with no newline), `read_line` returns `("", True)`, the caller can send a refusal, but calling `discard_line` to restore framing blocks forever in `stream.readline(65536)` waiting for a newline or EOF. That stalls the reader thread and prevents shutdown/cancel/other-frame processing. If the caller avoids `discard_line` to avoid the hang, the next `read_line` reads the remainder of the same oversize line as a new line, corrupting framing. The handling is memory-bounded but not time-bounded, so the original stall path remains through the new helper.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/mcpshim/wire.py:discard_line

chunk_findings.detail: The test writes 4000 bytes, waits for the `-32600` reply, and only then writes the terminating newline before checking that the shim can still serve `ping`. This does not exercise the hostile input that motivated the bounded-line fix: an oversize client line that is never terminated. If `discard_line` still blocks waiting for a newline/EOF up to a discard bound larger than the 4000 bytes the test sent, the shim’s reader thread is stalled after the error is written; a real client that sends the same 4000-byte prefix and then pauses keeps the reader blocked, so shutdown and other frames cannot be processed. The test passes because the test itself supplies the newline, giving false confidence that the stall is gone.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_mcp_soft_shim.py:test_an_oversize_line_is_refused_before_its_newline_arrives

chunk_findings.detail: A worker note whose `msg` is missing or not a dict still kills the reader. `{"t":"note"}` raises `KeyError` on `frame["msg"]`; `{"t":"note","msg":"hello"}` or `"msg": null` raises `AttributeError` on `msg.get` before the notification check. That callback is outside `route`'s new `try`, so the reader thread dies and every in-flight call, not just the bad frame, goes unanswered. The answer-shaped-note drop does not cover this input.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/mcpshim/shim.py:293

chunk_findings.detail: The earlier hostile-`res` defect still holds for a non-mapping `msg`. `{"t":"res","id":<worker id>,"msg":[]}` used to raise `AttributeError` on `reply.get`; `{**frame["msg"], "id": cid}` raises `TypeError` instead, still before any client write and still before `id` is replaced with `cid`. The pending call is never answered, and the same exception leaves the reader. `test_the_answer_carries_the_clients_id_whatever_the_worker_put_in_it` only covers a dict with a wrong id.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/mcpshim/shim.py:319

chunk_findings.detail:
`reap` closes stdin only if `wlock.acquire(timeout=2)` succeeds, and it never retries after the lock is free. A worker that has stopped reading fills the pipe; `send` blocks inside `write`/`flush` holding `wlock` for longer than 2s (stall timer not yet fired when `hello_timeout_s` is larger). `reap` then skips `stdin.close()`, waits, `kill()`s, and returns. After `kill` unblocks `send` and `wlock` is released, the write end stays open for the life of that `Popen`. Repeated stall-and-reap cycles leak pipe fds until a later spawn fails with `EMFILE`.

Previous items 1, 4, 6, 7, 8, 11, 12, and 14 are addressed by the new stall timer, floors, `stdin=DEVNULL` claim, and the route/cancel/error paths in this delta where those lines are visible. Items 9, 10, and 15 cannot be verified from this delta (tests and `find_repo` are not in this part). Items 2, 3, and 5 were rewritten; the residual non-dict frame crash and the stdin-close skip above are the new defects of that rewrite.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/mcpshim/child.py:87

chunk_findings.detail: The fallback that is supposed to turn an unencodable reply into a JSON-RPC error does not make the fallback itself JSON-safe: it reuses the original `obj["id"]` unsanitized and then serializes it with `json.dumps` using the default `allow_nan=True`. If the reply being written has a non-finite `id` (for example a forwarded worker frame whose JSON-RPC `id` is `1e999`, parsed by Python as `float("inf")`, or a direct call such as `shim.write({"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": float("nan"), "result": {}})`), the first `json.dumps(..., allow_nan=False)` raises `ValueError`, the fallback constructs `fail(nan_or_inf, ...)`, and the second `json.dumps` emits `NaN`/`Infinity` in the `id` field. The client then receives a non-JSON line instead of the promised typed error.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/mcpshim/shim.py:_write

chunk_findings.detail: `stalled` calls `self.kill()` while holding `guard`, and `send` holds `self.wlock` until after the `finally` that needs that same `guard`. `kill` takes `self.wlock` (its `finally` always `release`s it). A write that fills the pipe for `hello_timeout_s` and then completes — or a timer that fires as `flush` returns — interlocks: the timer thread sits in `kill` waiting for `wlock` while `send` sits in `finally` waiting for `guard`. The frame is never treated as sent or failed, the worker is not killed, and the in-flight call is left unanswered. The guard was meant to stop a late kill; it has to be dropped before `self.kill()`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/mcpshim/child.py:76

chunk_findings.detail: Cancellation no longer requires the same id type, only `cid == want and not isinstance(want, bool)`. In Python `1 == 1.0` and `1 == True` were the reason for the old `type(cid) is type(want)` check; dropping it keeps the bool hole closed but not the number hole. A pending call whose client id is `1` is marked answered-by-nobody when `notifications/cancelled` carries `"requestId": 1.0` (or the reverse), so the worker’s real result for that call is dropped and the client never sees it.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/mcpshim/shim.py:175
ddflow/mcpshim/wire.py:read_line

chunk_findings.detail: The new assertion `assert wire.read_line(io.StringIO("x" * 20 + "\n"), 10) == ("", wire.OVERSIZE_PENDING)` is wrong for the current `wire.read_line`: the line is complete (`complete` is `True`), its encoded size is 21, so `size - complete > limit` is true and the function returns `("", wire.OVERSIZE_DONE)`, not `OVERSIZE_PENDING`. This makes the new test fail on an input that is already a complete oversize line.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_mcp_soft_shim.py:960

chunk_findings.detail:
`test_read_line_reports_each_kind_of_oversize` asserts `wire.read_line(io.StringIO("x" * 20 + "
"), 10) == ("", wire.OVERSIZE_PENDING)`. That input is a finished line: `readline` returns `"x"*20+"
"`, `endswith("
")` is true, and `size - complete` is 20, which is over the limit, so `read_line` returns `("", OVERSIZE_DONE)`. The new test therefore fails on collect/run. Treating that frame as pending would also be the wrong contract: the newline was already consumed, so a caller that then `discard_line`s would drop the next message.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_mcp_soft_shim.py:959

data.command: $HOME/src/ddflow/.venv/bin/python3 -m ddflow --agent=lane-su review SU-shim --gate critic --delta --force --reason 'refresh after the byte-limit fix'

chunk_findings.detail: `Worker.send` arms the stall timer before `WP.encode(frame)` and then relies on `stall.cancel()` to avoid killing the worker. If encoding a frame takes longer than `hello_timeout_s` (for example, a large tool result near `max_line_bytes`), the timer can fire and call `self.kill()` before any bytes are written, killing a healthy worker even though the worker has not stopped reading. The opposite race is also possible: if the timer fires after `proc.stdin.flush()` succeeds but before `cancel()` can stop it, `send` returns `True` while the worker has just been killed, so the shim believes the frame was delivered and the corresponding call can go unanswered. The timeout should not include encoding, and a successful send must make the pending kill impossible (e.g. with a flag checked by the kill callback).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/mcpshim/child.py:71

chunk_findings.detail: `reap` closes `self.proc.stdout` while the reader thread may still be using that same text stream at line 45. For example, if a worker is alive but silent and the reader is blocked in `read_line`, a concurrent `reap()` call kills the child and then immediately calls `self.proc.stdout.close()` before the reader’s blocked read has necessarily returned EOF. Python text pipe objects are not safe for concurrent read/close; this interleaving can make `reap` block waiting on the reader’s I/O lock, or cause the reader to miss the frame/EOF and fail to call `on_exit` cleanly. `reap` should join the reader thread or otherwise ensure the reader has finished before closing `stdout`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/mcpshim/child.py:101

chunk_findings.detail: `math.isfinite(value)` is called on any JSON integer, but Python’s `math.isfinite` converts the int to a float and raises `OverflowError` for integers larger than the float maximum. A snapshot containing `{"limits": {"max_line_bytes": 1000000000000000000000000000000000000000}}` (or any 400-digit integer) makes `limits_for` raise instead of clamping the value to the 64 MiB ceiling. Because `limits_for` is used by the shim that fronts MCP connections, a hostile or corrupt snapshot can crash the shim during limits lookup, killing the agent’s tools; the clamp is supposed to cut above-ceiling values down to the ceiling.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/mcpshim/limits.py:clamp (line 50)

chunk_findings.detail: `route` special-cases notification methods without checking whether the message has an id. A JSON-RPC message that contains an id is a request and must receive a response. For example, given `{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":7,"method":"notifications/initialized"}`, `decode` returns the message, `route` hits the `notifications/initialized` branch and returns immediately, so no response for id `7` is ever written and the client hangs waiting. The same happens for `{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":7,"method":"notifications/cancelled",...}`: the cancellation side effect may run, but the request itself is never answered.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/mcpshim/shim.py:Shim.route

chunk_findings.detail: The shim uses Python’s default `json.loads`, which accepts non-finite numbers such as `NaN` and `Infinity`, and default `json.dumps`, which emits them as invalid JSON. Given the client request `{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":NaN,"method":"ping"}`, `decode` accepts it because the id is a float, `route` answers ping, and `write` emits `{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":NaN,"result":{}}`. A strict JSON-RPC/MCP client cannot parse `NaN`, causing protocol desync; the same occurs for `Infinity` and for forwarded requests whose ids are non-finite.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/mcpshim/shim.py:Shim.decode/Shim.write

chunk_findings.detail: Cancellation matching uses exact Python type equality, so JSON numbers that are numerically equal but serialized differently are not cancelled. If a pending request has id `1.0` and the client later sends `{"method":"notifications/cancelled","params":{"requestId":1}}`, `cid == want` is true but `type(cid) is type(want)` is false, so the request remains marked answered. When the worker later replies, the shim still sends the late answer to the client despite the cancellation.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/mcpshim/shim.py:Shim.cancel

chunk_findings.detail: The `--repo` argument is ignored when it is the last argument. The code uses `if "--repo" in args[:-1]`, so `ddflow-mcp --repo` (for example from an unquoted shell expansion where the repo variable is empty) does not produce a CLI error; it sets `repo_arg` to `""` and silently falls back to `DDFLOW_REPO` or the current working directory. That can make the shim operate on the wrong repository instead of rejecting the missing required argument.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/mcpshim/shim.py:main

chunk_findings.detail: `discard_line` loops on `stream.readline(65536)` until it sees a newline or EOF. Given the documented use—after `read_line` reports an over-limit line, the caller discards the rest—a peer can make the shim block for an unbounded amount of time: with `shim_max_line_bytes=1000`, a worker/agent sends 1001 bytes, then 100 MB of data without a newline (or simply keeps the connection open and waits for a response), and `discard_line` keeps reading forever. The shim cannot emit the over-limit error, restart the worker, or process other I/O while blocked, so the agent’s tools hang. The helper bounds memory but not the total bytes/time discarded and has no timeout/kill hook.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/mcpshim/wire.py:54 (`discard_line`)

chunk_findings.detail: The new snapshot-cache write is performed after `srv.handle(msg)` has already produced the JSON-RPC reply, but it is not guarded, and `srv.snapshot_due` is cleared only after the write succeeds. If `_snapfast.write_after` raises for any cache-level reason (for example, the snapshot directory is read-only, the disk is full, or the file cannot be serialized/written), the exception replaces the already-successful reply: the worker protocol answers the successful `initialize` as an internal error, and because `snapshot_due` remains set, the next request tries the same failing write again, so the worker keeps answering requests with internal errors or dies outright. This turns a snapshot-cache failure into a permanent loss of the agent's tools even though the MCP handler itself succeeded.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/worker.py (`handle` wrapper around `srv.handle`)

chunk_findings.detail: `deaf` mode is documented to “say hello and then never read stdin again,” but the implementation only sleeps 120 seconds after sending hello and then returns to the `for line in sys.stdin` loop. Given `FAKE_MODE=deaf` and a shim drain/hello timeout configured above 120 seconds (or a test that waits longer than 120 seconds), any `drain` or request frames sent while the worker is supposed to be deaf remain buffered and are processed after the sleep, causing late `drained`/responses. This both makes the deaf-worker timeout path hang for two minutes and can make the shim receive answers from a worker that should have been treated as dead.
chunk_findings.title: tests/fixtures/mcp_shim/fake_worker.py:112

chunk_findings.detail: `log` writes the request method verbatim followed by a newline, but the JSON-RPC method is an arbitrary string. Given a request whose method is `"foo\nstart"`, `log(f"req {method}")` writes two lines to `FAKE_LOG`: `req foo` and `start`. That violates the fixture’s “one line per started worker and per request” format and lets a hostile method forge a worker-start line in the log used by tests.
chunk_findings.title: tests/fixtures/mcp_shim/fake_worker.py:28

chunk_findings.detail: The test only asserts that the reply has `id == 1`; it never checks that the reply is a result/echo. If the shim rejects an odd `params` value with a JSON-RPC error that carries the request id (e.g. `{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"error":{"code":-32602}}` for `params={"_meta": 5}`), the assertion passes even though the request was not forwarded to the worker. The test can therefore false-pass the behavior its name claims to verify.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_mcp_soft_shim.py::test_odd_params_are_forwarded_for_the_worker_to_judge_not_a_crash

chunk_findings.detail: After forcing `on_frame` to raise for a `note` frame, the test checks only `c.recv()["id"] == 1`. If the shim catches the exception but answers the pending `progress` call with an internal error, the test still passes because the id matches; it does not assert that the first reply contains the worker's result/echo. Thus a lost or wrongly answered call can be accepted as a pass.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_mcp_soft_shim.py::test_a_bug_in_frame_handling_never_kills_the_reader_or_loses_the_call

chunk_findings.detail: The test sends `ping` after the cancellation sleep and reads only the first reply, then closes. If the cancelled request's answer is queued after the ping reply (for example, the worker subprocess/request forwarding is delayed past the 1.0s sleep and the shim still sends the late answer), the assertion passes because the first reply is the ping's. The test does not drain the queue or assert that no further frame for request id 5 arrives, so a late-answer bug can false-pass.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_mcp_soft_shim.py::test_a_cancelled_call_gets_no_late_answer

chunk_findings.detail: The test checks only captured stderr (`capfd.readouterr().err`) and ignores the fixture's worker log file (`c.log`, written via `FAKE_LOG`) that other tests use to inspect what the worker saw. If the fake worker logs request bodies to `FAKE_LOG`, the `SECRET-TOKEN-123` value sent in `params` will appear in `c.log`, but the test still passes because it never reads that log. A leak of message bodies into the worker log is therefore missed.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_mcp_soft_shim.py::test_message_bodies_never_reach_the_log

chunk_findings.detail: `Worker.send` arms `shim_hello_timeout_s` on every stdin write and kills the child if that write is still blocked when the timer fires. The knob is documented as only the wait for a started worker's hello, but a live worker that is inside a long tool and not reading stdin (normal single-threaded MCP stdio) will fill the OS pipe as soon as the shim forwards another frame larger than the remaining buffer. Example: hello timeout 30s, worker blocked 45s in `tools/call`, client sends a ~100KB follow-up; `write` blocks, the timer calls `kill()`, and the in-flight tool is destroyed even though the process was healthy. `stall.cancel()` does not stop a callback that has already started, so the same kill can run after `send` has already returned True.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/mcpshim/child.py:70

chunk_findings.detail: `build` does ` (getattr(server, "client_info", None) or {}).get("name", "")`. A live `initialize` can store `clientInfo` as a non-mapping (JSON string, list, or number). That value is truthy, so `.get` raises `AttributeError` before a snapshot is written. The worker path that writes the snapshot after initialize then dies, and the shim loses the agent's tools. A dict with a non-string `name` is already coerced to `""`; a non-dict `client_info` is not.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/ifacesnap.py:build

chunk_findings.detail: The new huge-int guard only clamps integers toward the ceiling, not toward the floor. For a snapshot limit such as `{"limits": {"max_line_bytes": -10**400}}`, `isinstance(value, int)` is true and `min(value, CEILINGS["max_line_bytes"])` returns the negative huge integer because it is below the ceiling. The next line evaluates `math.isfinite(num)` before `num < _FLOORS[key]`, so Python tries to convert the 400-digit negative int to a float and raises `OverflowError`. The same hostile or corrupt snapshot that motivated the positive-huge-int fix still crashes `limits_for` instead of dropping the value as below the floor.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/mcpshim/limits.py:clamp

chunk_findings.detail: The stall guard still can kill a worker after the frame has been successfully flushed. `stalled()` suppresses the kill only if it sees `finished` non-empty, but `finished` is appended in the `finally` after `flush()` returns. If the timer expires in the window after `self.proc.stdin.flush()` returns and before the `finally` acquires `guard`, the timer thread can enter `guard` first, see `finished` empty, and call `self.kill()`. A request whose write completed is then treated as successful by `send` while the worker is killed; for example, with `hello_timeout_s=0.1`, a slow-but-successful flush that finishes at 0.09999s can be preempted before the `finally`, and the timer kills a healthy worker.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/mcpshim/child.py:Worker.send

chunk_findings.detail: The new non-finite-number guard is bypassed by valid JSON numbers that overflow to infinity. `Shim.decode` now calls `json.loads(..., parse_constant=_no_constant)`, which only rejects the literal tokens `NaN`/`Infinity`; a request such as `{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1e999999,"method":"ping"}` is parsed by Python's float conversion into an `id` of `inf` and is accepted. `Shim.route` then calls `write` with `id=inf`; the first `json.dumps(..., allow_nan=False)` raises `ValueError`, but the fallback `json.dumps(fail(obj.get("id"), ...))` uses the default `allow_nan=True`, so it emits `Infinity` as the id in the error reply. The shim writes invalid JSON to the client and continues, causing protocol desync; the added probe for literal constants does not cover this overflowed-number input.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/mcpshim/shim.py:Shim.write

chunk_findings.detail: The huge-int guard only runs `min` against the ceiling, so a large negative integer is left intact and still hits `math.isfinite`. Given a snapshot `{"limits": {"max_line_bytes": -1000000000000000000000000000000000000000}}` (or any int below about `-1e308`), `num = min(value, CEILINGS[key])` is that negative int, `math.isfinite(num)` raises `OverflowError`, and `limits_for` still crashes the shim instead of skipping the value.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/mcpshim/limits.py:clamp

chunk_findings.detail: Non-finite values that never go through `parse_constant` still leave the wire. `json.loads("1e309")` becomes `inf` without calling `_no_constant`, so `{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1e309,"method":"ping"}` is accepted. `json.dumps(..., allow_nan=False)` then fails, and the fallback `json.dumps(fail(obj.get("id"), ...))` uses the default `allow_nan=True`, so the client is sent `Infinity` (invalid JSON) and desynchronizes. The same fallback emits `NaN` when a worker reply's id is already non-finite; if that second `dumps` raises, the outer `except` sets `gone` and writes nothing.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/mcpshim/shim.py:write

chunk_findings.detail: Encoding is no longer inside the timer, but a successful write can still kill the worker. `finished` is set only after `flush()` returns, and `Timer.cancel()` does not stop a callback that has already been scheduled. If `hello_timeout_s` elapses as `flush()` completes (floor is 0.1s; a large frame on a slow pipe), `stalled` can take `guard` first, see an empty `finished`, and call `self.kill()` on a worker that already accepted the frame.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/mcpshim/child.py:stalled

chunk_findings.detail: Dropping the type check makes JSON booleans match integers. `True == 1` and `True == 1.0` are true in Python, and the new condition only rejects a bool `want`. A pending request whose id is `true` is therefore marked answered by `{"method":"notifications/cancelled","params":{"requestId":1}}`, so its later reply is dropped; `requestId: true` does not cancel id `1`, so the match is also asymmetric.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/mcpshim/shim.py:cancel

chunk_findings.detail: `read_line` now advertises a byte limit, but it still obtains the line with `stream.readline(limit + 1)`, which waits for `limit + 1` characters (or a newline/EOF) before the encoded byte size is checked. With `max_line_bytes=1024`, a peer can send `"\u20ac" * 342` (1026 UTF-8 bytes) and no newline while keeping the stdin pipe open. The call blocks waiting for the 1025th character, so the shim never writes the `frame_too_large` error and cannot process further input; the byte ceiling has already been exceeded. The new tests only exercise complete oversize lines or ASCII pending lines, so they do not cover this incomplete multibyte case.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/mcpshim/wire.py:read_line

data.title: ddflow/mcpshim/wire.py:read_line

chunk_findings.detail: `Worker.send` arms the stall timer before `WP.encode(frame)` and then relies on `stall.cancel()` to avoid killing the worker. If encoding a frame takes longer than `hello_timeout_s` (for example, a large tool result near `max_line_bytes`), the timer can fire and call `self.kill()` before any bytes are written, killing a healthy worker even though the worker has not stopped reading. The opposite race is also possible: if the timer fires after `proc.stdin.flush()` succeeds but before `cancel()` can stop it, `send` returns `True` while the worker has just been killed, so the shim believes the frame was delivered and the corresponding call can go unanswered. The timeout should not include encoding, and a successful send must make the pending kill impossible (e.g. with a flag checked by the kill callback).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/mcpshim/child.py:71

chunk_findings.detail: `reap` closes `self.proc.stdout` while the reader thread may still be using that same text stream at line 45. For example, if a worker is alive but silent and the reader is blocked in `read_line`, a concurrent `reap()` call kills the child and then immediately calls `self.proc.stdout.close()` before the reader’s blocked read has necessarily returned EOF. Python text pipe objects are not safe for concurrent read/close; this interleaving can make `reap` block waiting on the reader’s I/O lock, or cause the reader to miss the frame/EOF and fail to call `on_exit` cleanly. `reap` should join the reader thread or otherwise ensure the reader has finished before closing `stdout`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/mcpshim/child.py:101

chunk_findings.detail: `math.isfinite(value)` is called on any JSON integer, but Python’s `math.isfinite` converts the int to a float and raises `OverflowError` for integers larger than the float maximum. A snapshot containing `{"limits": {"max_line_bytes": 1000000000000000000000000000000000000000}}` (or any 400-digit integer) makes `limits_for` raise instead of clamping the value to the 64 MiB ceiling. Because `limits_for` is used by the shim that fronts MCP connections, a hostile or corrupt snapshot can crash the shim during limits lookup, killing the agent’s tools; the clamp is supposed to cut above-ceiling values down to the ceiling.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/mcpshim/limits.py:clamp (line 50)

chunk_findings.detail: `route` special-cases notification methods without checking whether the message has an id. A JSON-RPC message that contains an id is a request and must receive a response. For example, given `{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":7,"method":"notifications/initialized"}`, `decode` returns the message, `route` hits the `notifications/initialized` branch and returns immediately, so no response for id `7` is ever written and the client hangs waiting. The same happens for `{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":7,"method":"notifications/cancelled",...}`: the cancellation side effect may run, but the request itself is never answered.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/mcpshim/shim.py:Shim.route

chunk_findings.detail: The shim uses Python’s default `json.loads`, which accepts non-finite numbers such as `NaN` and `Infinity`, and default `json.dumps`, which emits them as invalid JSON. Given the client request `{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":NaN,"method":"ping"}`, `decode` accepts it because the id is a float, `route` answers ping, and `write` emits `{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":NaN,"result":{}}`. A strict JSON-RPC/MCP client cannot parse `NaN`, causing protocol desync; the same occurs for `Infinity` and for forwarded requests whose ids are non-finite.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/mcpshim/shim.py:Shim.decode/Shim.write

chunk_findings.detail: Cancellation matching uses exact Python type equality, so JSON numbers that are numerically equal but serialized differently are not cancelled. If a pending request has id `1.0` and the client later sends `{"method":"notifications/cancelled","params":{"requestId":1}}`, `cid == want` is true but `type(cid) is type(want)` is false, so the request remains marked answered. When the worker later replies, the shim still sends the late answer to the client despite the cancellation.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/mcpshim/shim.py:Shim.cancel

chunk_findings.detail: The `--repo` argument is ignored when it is the last argument. The code uses `if "--repo" in args[:-1]`, so `ddflow-mcp --repo` (for example from an unquoted shell expansion where the repo variable is empty) does not produce a CLI error; it sets `repo_arg` to `""` and silently falls back to `DDFLOW_REPO` or the current working directory. That can make the shim operate on the wrong repository instead of rejecting the missing required argument.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/mcpshim/shim.py:main

chunk_findings.detail: `discard_line` loops on `stream.readline(65536)` until it sees a newline or EOF. Given the documented use—after `read_line` reports an over-limit line, the caller discards the rest—a peer can make the shim block for an unbounded amount of time: with `shim_max_line_bytes=1000`, a worker/agent sends 1001 bytes, then 100 MB of data without a newline (or simply keeps the connection open and waits for a response), and `discard_line` keeps reading forever. The shim cannot emit the over-limit error, restart the worker, or process other I/O while blocked, so the agent’s tools hang. The helper bounds memory but not the total bytes/time discarded and has no timeout/kill hook.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/mcpshim/wire.py:54 (`discard_line`)

chunk_findings.detail: The new snapshot-cache write is performed after `srv.handle(msg)` has already produced the JSON-RPC reply, but it is not guarded, and `srv.snapshot_due` is cleared only after the write succeeds. If `_snapfast.write_after` raises for any cache-level reason (for example, the snapshot directory is read-only, the disk is full, or the file cannot be serialized/written), the exception replaces the already-successful reply: the worker protocol answers the successful `initialize` as an internal error, and because `snapshot_due` remains set, the next request tries the same failing write again, so the worker keeps answering requests with internal errors or dies outright. This turns a snapshot-cache failure into a permanent loss of the agent's tools even though the MCP handler itself succeeded.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/worker.py (`handle` wrapper around `srv.handle`)

chunk_findings.detail: `deaf` mode is documented to “say hello and then never read stdin again,” but the implementation only sleeps 120 seconds after sending hello and then returns to the `for line in sys.stdin` loop. Given `FAKE_MODE=deaf` and a shim drain/hello timeout configured above 120 seconds (or a test that waits longer than 120 seconds), any `drain` or request frames sent while the worker is supposed to be deaf remain buffered and are processed after the sleep, causing late `drained`/responses. This both makes the deaf-worker timeout path hang for two minutes and can make the shim receive answers from a worker that should have been treated as dead.
chunk_findings.title: tests/fixtures/mcp_shim/fake_worker.py:112

chunk_findings.detail: `log` writes the request method verbatim followed by a newline, but the JSON-RPC method is an arbitrary string. Given a request whose method is `"foo\nstart"`, `log(f"req {method}")` writes two lines to `FAKE_LOG`: `req foo` and `start`. That violates the fixture’s “one line per started worker and per request” format and lets a hostile method forge a worker-start line in the log used by tests.
chunk_findings.title: tests/fixtures/mcp_shim/fake_worker.py:28

chunk_findings.detail: The test only asserts that the reply has `id == 1`; it never checks that the reply is a result/echo. If the shim rejects an odd `params` value with a JSON-RPC error that carries the request id (e.g. `{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"error":{"code":-32602}}` for `params={"_meta": 5}`), the assertion passes even though the request was not forwarded to the worker. The test can therefore false-pass the behavior its name claims to verify.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_mcp_soft_shim.py::test_odd_params_are_forwarded_for_the_worker_to_judge_not_a_crash

chunk_findings.detail: After forcing `on_frame` to raise for a `note` frame, the test checks only `c.recv()["id"] == 1`. If the shim catches the exception but answers the pending `progress` call with an internal error, the test still passes because the id matches; it does not assert that the first reply contains the worker's result/echo. Thus a lost or wrongly answered call can be accepted as a pass.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_mcp_soft_shim.py::test_a_bug_in_frame_handling_never_kills_the_reader_or_loses_the_call

chunk_findings.detail: The test sends `ping` after the cancellation sleep and reads only the first reply, then closes. If the cancelled request's answer is queued after the ping reply (for example, the worker subprocess/request forwarding is delayed past the 1.0s sleep and the shim still sends the late answer), the assertion passes because the first reply is the ping's. The test does not drain the queue or assert that no further frame for request id 5 arrives, so a late-answer bug can false-pass.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_mcp_soft_shim.py::test_a_cancelled_call_gets_no_late_answer
